words.note: Book headword pinyin printed as kěnéng. Example-sentence pinyin not printed in the book; standard pinyin added. Pairing in book: 可能会变. Avoid: 可能 is not a promise — do not let the other person treat it as already certain.
words.when: Remember 可能 like the word you’ll use when you mark possibility without claiming you know the outcome — useful when workplace data is still incomplete.
words.usage: Most Chinese speakers hedge schedules and outcomes with 可能 / 可能会… so the listener hears uncertainty, not a locked plan. In office talk it softens forecasts (明天的时间可能会变). Never let a 可能 reply stand alone if the other side needs a firm yes/no.

example.pinyin: Míngtiān de shíjiān kěnéng huì biàn.

words.note: Book headword pinyin printed as dàgài. Example-sentence pinyin not printed in the book; standard pinyin added. Pairing in book: 大概十分钟. Avoid: for dates or numbers that must be exact, do not use 大概 without saying it is only an estimate.
words.when: Remember 大概 like the word you’ll use when you give an approximate number, time, or rough picture — not a contractual figure.
words.usage: Most Chinese speakers put 大概 before a duration or quantity (大概十分钟, 大概半个小时) for a ballpark. It is fine for planning talk; flag that it is approximate when accuracy matters (deadlines, invoices, signed dates).

example.zh: 这个会大概需要半个小时。
example.pinyin: Zhège huì dàgài xūyào bàn ge xiǎoshí.
example.en: This meeting will take about half an hour.

words.note: Book headword pinyin printed as yīnggāi. Example-sentence pinyin not printed in the book; standard pinyin added. Pairing in book: 应该没问题. Avoid: do not use 应该 to claim you have verified something — it is still your judgment.
words.when: Remember 应该 like the word you’ll use when you state a duty or a fairly strong guess — context decides which reading listeners hear.
words.usage: Most Chinese speakers use 应该 for obligation (“should”) or a confident inference (“should already be there / should be fine”: 应该没问题). In status updates it still means assessment, not verified fact. If you checked the system, say what you checked instead of only 应该.

words.note: Book headword pinyin printed as gūjì. Example-sentence pinyin not printed in the book; standard pinyin added. Pairing in book: 估计来不及. Avoid: 估计 marks an estimate, not a final number already agreed.
words.when: Remember 估计 like the word you’ll use when you guess from the information you have — a natural workplace forecast, not a locked figure.
words.usage: Most Chinese speakers open with 我估计… to own a personal forecast (我估计今天做不完, 估计来不及). It sounds collaborative and honest about uncertainty. Do not treat an 估计 as the signed-off number in a plan or contract.

example.pinyin: Wǒ gūjì jīntiān zuò bu wán.
example.en: I reckon we won’t finish today.

words.note: Book headword pinyin printed as hǎoxiàng. Example-sentence pinyin not printed in the book; standard pinyin added. Pairing in book: 好像有变化. Avoid: 好像 can sound weak for an official report — verify first if a decision depends on it.
words.when: Remember 好像 like the word you’ll use when you share an impression from what you observed but have not confirmed yet.
words.usage: Most Chinese speakers soften tentative reads with 好像 (他好像还没收到消息, 好像有变化). Fine in chat and stand-ups; too soft alone for formal reports or decisions that need verified status — check, then upgrade the language.

example.pinyin: Tā hǎoxiàng hái méi shōudào xiāoxi.
example.en: It seems he hasn’t received the message yet.

words.note: Book headword pinyin printed as chàbuduō. Example-sentence pinyin not printed in the book; standard pinyin added. Pairing in book: 差不多完成了. Avoid: 差不多 is not “exactly the same”; do not use it for contract numbers.
words.when: Remember 差不多 like the word you’ll use when a number, time, or condition is close enough — arrival around ten, work almost done.
words.usage: Most Chinese speakers use 差不多 for nearness (我们差不多十点到, 差不多完成了). It signals “close, not exact.” Keep it out of contracts, invoices, and other figures that must match precisely.

words.note: Book headword pinyin printed as yǒudiǎn. Example-sentence pinyin not printed in the book; standard pinyin added. Pairing in book: 有点难. Avoid: 有点 often carries a negative shade; for positive praise prefer 比较 or 很.
words.when: Remember 有点 like the word you’ll use when you soften a less-than-ideal assessment — the schedule is a bit tight, the task a bit hard.
words.usage: Most Chinese speakers soften mild complaints with 有点 + adjective (有点紧, 有点难). It usually leans negative or imperfect. For praise or a positive comparison, the book points you to 比较 or 很 instead.

example.en: This timing is a bit tight.

words.note: Book headword pinyin printed as bǐjiào. Example-sentence pinyin not printed in the book; standard pinyin added. Pairing in book: 比较合适. Avoid: 比较 can mean “relatively”; do not auto-translate as “more” without a comparison object.
words.when: Remember 比较 like the word you’ll use when you rate something without sounding extreme — a calm way to prefer one option over another.
words.usage: Most Chinese speakers use 比较 + adjective for a moderate judgment (这个方案比较合适). It often means “relatively / fairly,” not a hard comparative “more … than …” unless a second object is clear. Good for soft option talk in meetings.

words.note: Book headword pinyin printed as tèbié. Example-sentence pinyin not printed in the book; standard pinyin added. Pairing in book: 特别重要. Avoid: 特别 also means “special / particular”; watch position and context.
words.when: Remember 特别 like the word you’ll use when you need stronger everyday emphasis than 很 — today is especially busy, this is particularly important.
words.usage: Most Chinese speakers intensify with 特别 (今天特别忙, 特别重要), stronger than plain 很 in casual speech. The same word can mean “special” as an adjective — read position and context so you do not mix “especially busy” with “a special case.”

example.zh: 今天特别忙，我们明天再聊吧。
example.pinyin: Jīntiān tèbié máng, wǒmen míngtiān zài liáo ba.
example.en: Today is especially busy — let’s talk again tomorrow.

words.note: Book headword pinyin printed as bú tài (tone sandhi on 不). Example-sentence pinyin not printed in the book; standard pinyin added. Pairing in book: 不太方便. Avoid: 不太 is not an absolute refusal — if something is impossible, say so clearly.
words.when: Remember 不太 like the word you’ll use for a polite soft no — mild mismatch or inconvenience without slamming the door.
words.usage: Most Chinese speakers refuse gently with 不太 + adjective (不太方便) and often offer an alternative (明天可以吗？). It leaves room to renegotiate. If the ask is truly impossible, explain firmly instead of only 不太.

example.zh: 今天下午不太方便，明天可以吗？
example.pinyin: Jīntiān xiàwǔ bú tài fāngbiàn, míngtiān kěyǐ ma?
example.en: This afternoon isn’t very convenient — is tomorrow okay?

notes.title: Certainty ladder: 可能 / 好像 / 估计 / 应该
notes.body: Module 05 asks you to separate guess, estimate, judgment, and mild complaint so workplace meaning lands correctly. 可能 marks possibility without claiming the result (not a promise). 好像 shares an unconfirmed impression and can sound weak in official reports. 估计 is a forecast from available information, not a final agreed number. 应该 can mean duty or a fairly strong guess — still your assessment, not verified fact (pairing: 应该没问题).

example.pinyin: Míngtiān de shíjiān kěnéng huì biàn.

notes.title: Approximate time and quantity: 大概 / 差不多
notes.body: 大概 frames ballpark numbers and durations (大概十分钟, 大概半个小时). 差不多 marks nearness of time, number, or condition (差不多十点, 差不多完成了). Neither means exact identity — the book warns against using them for dates or figures that must be accurate, especially contract numbers.

example.zh: 这个会大概需要半个小时。
example.pinyin: Zhège huì dàgài xūyào bàn ge xiǎoshí.
example.en: This meeting will take about half an hour.

notes.title: Intensity without extremes: 有点 / 比较 / 特别 / 不太
notes.body: 有点 softens a less-than-ideal take and often leans negative (有点紧, 有点难); for positive praise the book prefers 比较 or 很. 比较 rates degree without sounding extreme (比较合适) and often means “relatively,” not automatic “more … than ….” 特别 is stronger everyday emphasis than 很 (特别忙 / 特别重要) and can also mean “special.” 不太 is a polite soft refusal (不太方便), not an absolute no — if it is impossible, say so clearly.

example.zh: 今天下午不太方便，明天可以吗？
example.pinyin: Jīntiān xiàwǔ bú tài fāngbiàn, míngtiān kěyǐ ma?
example.en: This afternoon isn’t very convenient — is tomorrow okay?

notes.title: Latihan 90 detik (book exercise)
notes.body: Book drill on p.20: pick three entries from this module — 可能, 好像, and 特别 — and build one work or daily story that uses all three. Record without reading the PDF, then check whether your timing and decisions came out clearly. No model Chinese dialogue is printed for this drill; do not invent one as book text.

example.zh: 可能 / 好像 / 特别
example.en: Target trio for the 90-second practice (instruction only; no sample story in the book).
